summary: Research why players love watching sims/systemic games and turn it into concrete VIRAL mechanisms

principles.principle: Only what reaches the player's head counts: make cognition legible, not deeper
principles.why_it_works: Watchers enjoy simulations through the mental model the game projects into them. Interesting internal state the viewer never perceives is wasted. VIRAL's best material is in its JSON: the gap between what was said, what was understood, what the character believes and how sure they are. Today most of that stays hidden in a caption sub-line.
principles.evidence: Sylvester's 'Simulation Dream' separates the Game Model (code) from the Player Model (what the player perceives) and argues that complexity which never reaches the player is wasted. He recommends simulating only what players can perceive and leaning on familiar archetypes. RimWorld cut Dwarf Fortress's layered systems down to a small cast of colonists with few, high-impact traits so players can observe and understand them.

principles.principle: Apophenia: the viewer co-authors the story from small, readable cues
principles.why_it_works: People read intention and emotion into very simple motion: a hurry, a pause, turning toward someone. Will Wright calls this offloading the simulation into the player's imagination, or 'parallel processing'. A low-poly resident who hesitates, then hurries off, reads as a decision without any extra AI.
principles.evidence: Sylvester cites the Michotte/Heider-Simmel moving-shapes experiments and a Sims 3 anecdote as apophenia doing the storytelling. Wright says he wants to 'build the maximum possibility space in your head, not on the computer', and that players switch between 'me' and 'him' when a Sim rebels. Two Point's animators aim for 'as much expression and character as we can' in every little person.

principles.principle: Suspense beats surprise: show the bomb under the table
principles.why_it_works: Tension comes from the audience knowing something the characters do not, then watching the clock. In VIRAL the player knows the sentence was false or a joke, and knows who has just heard it. A pending model call is a ticking clock. Showing 'X just heard Y and is now thinking...' turns 5-40 s of latency from dead air into anticipation, and the decision becomes the payoff.
principles.evidence: Hitchcock to Truffaut: a bomb that explodes with no warning gives a few seconds of surprise. If the audience is shown the bomb and the clock first, the same scene holds 15 minutes of suspense, so 'the public must be informed' whenever possible. Disney's 'anticipation' principle makes the same point at the scale of a single motion.

principles.principle: Peaks and valleys: alternate build-up, a held peak and relief
principles.why_it_works: Constant intensity numbs viewers, and so do constant lulls. A peak lands because a quiet stretch came before it, and the quiet after a peak lets the viewer take in what changed. VIRAL cannot invent events, but the playback director fully controls timing: compressing low-stakes beats, holding on big real changes, and giving each one a breath.
principles.evidence: Booth's Left 4 Dead AI Director estimates player intensity and cycles through Build Up, Sustain Peak (3-5 s after the peak), Peak Fade (wait for a natural break) and Relax (30-45 s of minimal threat). The slides argue that unpredictable peaks and valleys create a powerfully compelling experience. RimWorld's Cassandra alternates on-phases and off-phases with a minimum gap between major threats, and Sylvester cites the Left 4 Dead Director as the storyteller's model.

principles.principle: Make the spread one glanceable, growing quantity, with an opposing force
principles.why_it_works: In Plague Inc, the map filling with red dots is the story. A single monotonic visual (spread) plus an opposing one (the cure) creates a race the viewer can follow without reading anything. Milestone comparisons give scale and a joke. In VIRAL the opposing force is real too: residents who inspect and find nothing, or who doubt.
principles.evidence: Kotaku describes red dots spreading as you infect more people, and milestone alerts that compare your disease to the common cold or the Black Death. The CDC issues news headlines that narrate the world's response. Vaughan calls the game a heavily algorithmic world-response model that is surfaced through these channels.

principles.principle: Show the cause next to the effect, like RimWorld's mood thoughts
principles.why_it_works: Lines like 'Saw corpse -5' make an invisible state change attributable. The viewer can trace a chain of causes, and that traceability is what lets them later say 'it ended up like this because...'. Attributed causes are also funny when the cause is petty and the effect is big.
principles.evidence: RimWorld lists every mood modifier with its source and value (from memory; the wiki was not re-fetched). Sylvester designs incidents to overlap and interact so that causes chain. Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023) showed a party invitation spreading from one seed agent through a town, and rendered each agent's current state as an emoji over its avatar so the diffusion was readable.

principles.principle: Comedy comes from consistent characters failing in everyday ways, exaggerated so it reads from a distance, with bystanders reacting
principles.why_it_works: Sims and Two Point humour is rarely a written joke. It is a readable personality meeting a mundane situation, plus the reactions of everyone around it. In VIRAL the richest comic contrast is between what a character says out loud and what they privately think: both are real model outputs.
principles.evidence: Two Point devs exaggerated the slip animation because it 'needs to be visible from a distance'. They also note that small bystander behaviours, such as people reacting to vomit in the room, add to the humour. Some ailments start as visual gags. Richard Evans (Sims 3 AI lead) set the goal that each Sim's personality be 'clearly manifest in autonomous behavior'. Simlish gibberish lets players project their own meaning onto conversations.

principles.principle: Emergent stories need a curator: the recounting is what gets shared
principles.why_it_works: Raw simulation logs are dull. A story exists once someone selects and recounts the chain. Dwarf Fortress has Legends mode and player write-ups, RimWorld has Reddit tales, and The Sims had the Sims Exchange where players uploaded families and stories. A deterministic recap built from validated events gives the player the 'one sentence led to THIS' artifact to share, without inventing anything.
principles.evidence: Ryan's dissertation argues that emergent narrative fails without curation and frames story generation as recounting rather than invention. Wright describes mining Sims Exchange uploads. Tarn Adams says the story tools are meant to let players produce their own stories.

principles.principle: Losing is fun: frame the fizzle as an outcome, and surface the near-miss
principles.why_it_works: A rumour that dies is realistic, but it feels flat when it ends with no framing. Dwarf Fortress makes failure the content. Near-misses ('it almost happened') raise the urge to try again more than clear losses do. VIRAL already has the real data for this: low-confidence stances, validator rejections, and actions not taken.
principles.evidence: Dwarf Fortress's official motto is 'Losing is fun!' and the game has no win condition (Adams on SE Daily; the Game Developer making-of). In near-miss studies, near-misses recruit reward circuitry and increase the desire to play, even though they are losses (Clark et al. 2009, Neuron; cited from memory).

principles.principle: Juice is earned emphasis: small feedback on every beat, big feedback only on peaks
principles.why_it_works: Squash and stretch, pops, sound stings and camera moves make events feel consequential. If every event gets a big effect, nothing stands out and the pacing curve flattens. Tying effect strength to an event's real tier keeps the presentation honest and the rhythm readable. Cadence target for VIRAL: a micro-beat every 1.5-3 s, a turn (someone new hears, believes or flips) every 8-15 s, and a held peak whenever a world-visible change really occurs.
principles.evidence: In 'Juice it or lose it' (Jonasson and Purho), the same game becomes far more alive with tweening, squash and particles alone. In 'The Art of Screenshake' (Nijman/Vlambeer), feedback is layered, but its strength is matched to impact. Both talks cited from memory.

mechanisms.name: Thinking beat (latency becomes suspense)
mechanisms.what: While a model call for resident X is pending (the engine frontier is ahead of playback, or X has heard a message and has no 'decide' yet): (1) CameraRig in src/town/TownScene.tsx slowly dollies toward X (lerp k≈0.02/frame). (2) X does a procedural ponder idle in PlaybackLayer: head-yaw oscillation of ±15° at 0.4 Hz, a 0.6 m pace loop, and a slight y-scale breathe. (3) A '💭' bubble shows animated dots. (4) The HUD shows 'X 正在想…' with an elapsed-seconds counter, plus the 'bomb': the exact line X just heard and who said it (real deliver event). (5) A WebAudio low sine drone rises in pitch and gain over 0-20 s (cap −24 dB). When the decide event arrives: the drone cuts, a 'pop' (short noise burst plus 880 Hz blip) plays, the bubble bursts into emoji(out.feeling), and the camera holds 1 s before the decision caption.
mechanisms.serves: Suspense beats surprise; peaks and valleys (build-up into release)
mechanisms.risks: A 40 s wait still drags: auto-cut to other pending real events or a wide town shot after about 12 s, then return. The drone can annoy, so add a mute toggle. Never show a fake progress percentage.

mechanisms.name: Telephone-game diff with a 'because' line
mechanisms.what: On every talk/phone/notice/article caption, show the version being passed on and highlight what changed versus the version this speaker received. Use a char-level LCS diff on the Chinese strings (≈40 lines): inserted chars bold or colored, dropped chars struck through. Under each decision caption add a RimWorld-style cause line built only from the real triggering message: '相信 72% ← 王太太電話裡說「…」'. Implement in director.ts caption() by adding a 'diff' field and a 'cause' field to Caption.
mechanisms.serves: Legibility of cognition; showing the cause next to the effect; humour of distortion ('how did it end up like this')
mechanisms.risks: Paraphrases diff noisily: fall back to showing the 'received' and 'passed on' lines stacked when similarity is below 0.3. Truncate quotes to about 24 chars.

mechanisms.name: Says vs thinks split
mechanisms.what: When a resident acts (tell/phone/statement), show the speech bubble with what they say and, at the same moment, a smaller grey thought bubble with out.thought. When the stance confidence is below 0.5 but the action still spreads the claim, tint the pair amber and tag it '半信半疑卻照傳' (an honest mismatch computed from real fields). Optionally, when feeling and spoken tone diverge (e.g. feeling 😒, speech polite), show the feeling emoji on the thought side only.
mechanisms.serves: Comedy from consistent characters (gap between inner self and public face); legibility; dramatic irony
mechanisms.risks: Screen clutter during multi-person scenes: show the split only for the focused actor and keep other residents to an emoji.

mechanisms.name: Intensity tiers drive pacing (peak hold and relax)
mechanisms.what: In src/sim/timing.ts add tierOf(e): 0 = move, deliver, background; 1 = talk, phone, look, decide; 2 = notice, article, statement, shop state; 3 = cancel festival, police, close stage, rally. Playback rules: tier 0 plays at 1.6× speed. Tier ≥2 gets a Sustain Peak hold of +3 s (tier 3: +5 s), a camera push-in, a low-tom sting and the world prop popping in with squash. Then a 2-3 s Relax wide shot of the area before the next event. Never insert holds between two tier-0 events. Cap total added hold at 20% of story length.
mechanisms.serves: Peaks and valleys; juice as earned emphasis
mechanisms.risks: Stories with no tier-2+ events have no peak, which the fizzle framing on the recap card has to cover. Tune holds against the existing watchSeconds so a 16-decision story does not exceed about 60 s.

mechanisms.name: Recap card: '一句話的後果' (curated share artifact)
mechanisms.what: Build a deterministic end card from validated events only, with no LLM summary. Top: the player's sentence and target. Middle: a chain strip of portrait chips (player → A → B → C), each with its received/passed-on mini-quote, the belief % and the diff highlight; the branch where a chain forks shows two rows. Bottom: the biggest real outcome as a headline (from tierOf, e.g. '燈籠節取消了'), plus counts: people reached, believers, doubters, model decisions, game minutes elapsed. Buttons: 'copy story text' (plain-text chain for chat apps) and 'save image' (canvas toDataURL with preserveDrawingBuffer, or draw the card onto a 2D canvas). Also 'Try again: same person / another person'.
mechanisms.serves: Curation (recounting is what gets shared); sharing; retry
mechanisms.risks: Long chains overflow the card: show the top 5 hops and collapse the rest into '+N 人'. The image path may be slow; ship text copy first.

mechanisms.name: Fizzle as punchline and near-miss
mechanisms.what: When a story ends with no tier-2+ event, the recap card frames the ending instead of reading 'ended'. Pick, from real data, (a) the most dramatic action that was considered but rejected by the validator (the 'rejected' events), or (b) the highest-confidence stance that did not lead to an action, and print it as a near-miss: '陳警官差點出動（信心 0.48）' or '林老闆想關店，但鎮長不准'. Add a deadpan fixed-template title by outcome type ('謠言死於午餐時間'). Then offer 'Tell it to <the person the last believer is closest to>' using the real relationship table, worded as a suggestion and never as a prediction.
mechanisms.serves: Losing is fun (near-miss); retry motivation
mechanisms.risks: If no near-miss exists, show the most doubtful reaction ('沒人信你，王太太覺得你怪怪的') from real stance data. Never claim what would have happened.

mechanisms.name: Spread meter and belief rings
mechanisms.what: Top-HUD Plague-style bar: counts of 聽說 / 相信 / 懷疑 that tick up with a soft pop and count-up animation on each real deliver/stance change. Above involved residents, a thin ring: color by stance (red believes, blue doubts, grey unaware) and arc length = confidence. Optional opposing 'truth' segment that grows only when a real inspect/look event reports the claim unsupported. Milestone toast at 3, 5 and 8 people ('已經比菜市場八卦傳得還快'), from fixed text.
mechanisms.serves: One glanceable spread quantity with an opposing force; anticipation (watching the number climb)
mechanisms.risks: Rings for 90 townsfolk would add noise: show them on the 8 named residents only. Milestone jokes must not imply a fake comparison with real data; keep them clearly playful.

mechanisms.name: Procedural body language and per-resident gait
mechanisms.what: A small set of reusable r3f tweens on the existing agent groups, driven only by real event fields. React-jump on hearing news: y-scale 0.85→1.12→1 over 0.3 s. Lean-in during talk: 8° pitch and 0.3 m toward the partner. Hurry when the chosen action is urgent (stance confidence >0.8 or feeling in an anger/fear set): walk ×1.5 with a higher bob frequency. Slump when the decision is 'do nothing': y-scale 0.95, slow turn away. Bystanders within 6 m turn their heads toward a talk or phone. Each named resident gets fixed gait params (bob amplitude, sway, speed, head-tilt habit) so they are recognisable from far away.
mechanisms.serves: Apophenia (readable intent); comedy readable from a distance
mechanisms.risks: Performance: apply to named residents and the 10 nearest townsfolk only. Avoid emotion poses that contradict the model's feeling.

mechanisms.name: Bystander reactions to real world changes
mechanisms.what: When a tier-2+ world prop appears (stage tape, notice, police car, closed shop sign), 3-6 nearest background townsfolk stop, face it, show a '❓/😮' bubble for 2 s, and 1-2 of them linger 5 s before resuming their routine. Render them without threads or captions, and do not count them in the spread meter. Write a code comment: ambient presentation, not causal.
mechanisms.serves: Comedy from bystander reactions (Two Point); making the world feel the consequence
mechanisms.risks: Viewers might read it as rumour spreading to them. Keep their bubbles neutral (curiosity) and never show speech.

mechanisms.name: Gibberish voice and sound stings (WebAudio)
mechanisms.what: Simlish/Animalese-style blips: for each displayed speech character, play a 45 ms triangle-oscillator blip at the resident's base pitch ±3 semitones (8 fixed voice profiles), at most 12 blips per second. Phone voices go through a 300-3000 Hz bandpass. Thoughts are silent apart from a soft 'hmm' glide. Stings: pop for a new believer, paper rustle (filtered noise) for a notice or article, low tom for a tier-3 change, rising drone for the thinking beat. One master gain plus a mute toggle.
mechanisms.serves: Personality readable without text; earned emphasis; pacing rhythm
mechanisms.risks: Gets annoying fast: duck blips when captions are long and keep the master level low. The AudioContext must start on the first click (browser autoplay policy).

mechanisms.name: Town news ticker (Plague headlines and Two Point radio voice)
mechanisms.what: A bottom ticker that rewrites only real events into headline voice, from 2-3 deterministic templates per event type filled with names and quotes ('快訊｜廣場布告欄出現新公告：「…」', '本報記者：鎮長表示「…」'). Between stories, play 6-8 fixed flavour lines in a radio-DJ voice that reference no current event.
mechanisms.serves: Spread made legible; humour; a recap of what happened for viewers who glanced away
mechanisms.risks: Template repetition; keep it short. Ticker lines must match a real event id so nothing is invented.

mechanisms.name: Act titles at real thresholds
mechanisms.what: Flash a 1.2 s title card when a real threshold is first crossed: first retelling ('第一幕：傳出去了'), first phone call ('消息上了電話線'), first public act such as a notice or article ('第二幕：全鎮都會知道'), first institutional act such as police or festival ('第三幕：事情鬧大了'), and end. Derive the thresholds from event types.
mechanisms.serves: Peaks and valleys (structure and anticipation); curation
mechanisms.risks: Interrupts flow if it appears too often: at most 3 per story.

mechanisms.name: Camera grammar for talk and phone
mechanisms.what: Talk: a two-shot framing both residents from the side at the midpoint, with the camera at 1.6× their separation. Phone: a picture-in-picture inset (second r3f View or a small render target) showing the listener while the main view stays on the caller, replacing the hard cut halfway. Peak: push-in. Relax: pull back to a wide shot.
mechanisms.serves: Legibility (who is talking to whom); peaks and valleys
mechanisms.risks: A second render view costs frames on low-end laptops; fall back to the current cut.

mechanisms.name: One-tap prediction before playback
mechanisms.what: After the sentence is entered, an optional chip row with fixed choices, '你猜會傳到幾個人？ 1 / 2-4 / 5+'. The recap card reveals hit or miss. No scoring or persistence.
mechanisms.serves: Anticipation (a reason to watch for a specific outcome); retry
mechanisms.risks: Adds a step before the payoff: make it skippable and default to skip.

avoid: Padding runtime: slow walks, repeated establishing shots, or unskippable holds. Always offer 2× speed and 'skip to recap'.

Any presentation that implies a cause the engine did not produce: bystanders 'spreading' the rumour, headlines about events that did not happen, or thinking previews that hint at a decision before the model returns.
An LLM-written recap or ticker. Every recounted line must come from validated events or fixed templates.
A spinner or fake progress bar during model calls. Show who is thinking and what they just heard instead.
Juice inflation: shake, stings or push-ins on every event. Reserve big feedback for tier-2+ events so peaks stay legible.
Showing the state of all 90 townsfolk, or long model text. Captions should be one line plus one sub-line, with quotes trimmed to about 24 chars.
Ending a fizzled story with a bare 'ended'. Without framing and a near-miss, a short story reads as broken rather than realistic.
Adding goals, scores, unlocks, progression or multi-sentence turns that extend playtime and dilute the one-sentence premise.
Constant music or a constant drone. Silence in relax beats is part of the pacing.
Explaining the joke with labels like 'funny!'. Let the diff and the says-vs-thinks contrast carry the humour.

principles.principle: Hidden state counts for nothing: every real decision has to show up in posture, gaze, gesture or a one-line caption at the moment it is made
principles.why_it_works: Viewers judge intelligence and intent from what they can perceive. By default an LLM's cognition is invisible: a resident who just walks over looks scripted. One who stops, frowns, glances at the bakery and then strides off looks like they decided something, so the player credits the model with it.
principles.evidence: Bungie's Halo AI talk lists 'Discarded: Hidden States' under 'Making the AI Intelligible'. In its place: inform the player through language, posture, gesture and focus of attention. It also names 'Subtlety' as a thing to avoid. In playtests the same AI read as 'very intelligent' to 43% of players when enemies were tougher, against 8% when they were weak, so perceived smartness follows what players see. Sylvester argues that anything in the game model that doesn't reach the player's mental model is worthless, citing Ultima Online's unnoticed ecology.
sources: Butcher & Griesemer, 'The Illusion of Intelligence', GDC 2002 slides — https://www.jmeiners.com/shamans/papers/ai/the_illusion_of_intelligence.pdf

principles.principle: Telegraph intent before the act (anticipation), so the walk to the target becomes suspense rather than transit
principles.why_it_works: Suspense comes from the audience knowing what is about to happen before it does (Hitchcock's 'bomb under the table'). In Hitman the fun is watching a set-up chain trigger: NPCs are predictable, so you can foresee and savour the moment. In VIRAL, once the JSON says 'phone the Mayor', showing that intent first turns 15 seconds of walking into 'oh no, she's going to the Mayor'.
principles.evidence: In Hitman, routines must be 'predictable and reliable'. Animation telegraphs a character's intent. Targets do specific things once the world changes because those behaviours are tied to their goals, which is why they walk into the player's set-ups. Halo's design goals include a 'transparent thought process' and 'communication of intent'. Anticipation is one of Disney's 12 principles.

principles.principle: The reaction is the punchline: the joke lands on the person who hears it, not the one who says it
principles.why_it_works: Slapstick needs a straight man. The goose stealing a rake isn't funny until the gardener notices it's gone. Reactions also confirm causality ('my sentence did that') and show scale: one head turning is gossip, thirty heads turning is a scandal.
principles.evidence: House House gave NPCs separate AI states for 'noticed something missing' and 'spotted the goose'. They found stealing while people weren't looking was funnier than plain grabbing, and that 'the conflict is always easy to read'. Halo's 'Impressed' goal is reacting to the player with surprise, anger or awe. Hitman's crowds use 'behaviour zones', pulses with a radius and angle that make agents look at a point of interest, become alert or panic, and they never calm down once set off.
sources: Road to the IGF: Untitled Goose Game — https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/road-to-the-igf-house-house-s-i-untitled-goose-game-i-

principles.principle: A legible everyday routine is the baseline that makes a deviation readable and funny
principles.why_it_works: You only notice 'something happened to Tom' if you know what Tom normally does. Mundane routines also give the comic contrast: a sweeper who drops the broom to phone the police is funnier than a generic NPC who sprints.
principles.evidence: Hitman's AI is built on interruptible routines (serving drinks, guarding doors). Some interruptions draw characters at once and others are delayed, tuned per action. Kotaku made a compilation of one random Sapienza NPC's phone calls because watching an ordinary routine was entertaining in itself. IOI describes the overheard 'seedy stories' as a core strength. They play out whether or not you listen.
sources: Kotaku, 'The Hidden Life of a Random Hitman NPC' — https://kotaku.com/the-hidden-life-of-a-random-hitman-npc-1773218201

principles.principle: Dramatic irony through mutation: the player knows the original sentence, so watching it get distorted hop by hop is the core joke and the 'how did it end up like THIS' moment
principles.why_it_works: The goose game's comedy is knowing what the gardener doesn't. In VIRAL, the player is the only one who knows the true source and wording. Each retelling that drifts (topic change, more confidence, a new villain) is a small punchline only they get. The drift is real model output, so it is emergent, not faked.
principles.evidence: Goose: theft while unseen beats overt theft, so the comedy runs on the gap between what the audience knows and what the characters know. Sylvester's Sims 3 example: a simple attraction mechanic became a jealousy-and-revenge story because players projected meaning onto it. Hitman's private knowledge bases and stale shared info ('information can go stale') create openings because NPCs act on outdated beliefs.
sources: Road to the IGF: Untitled Goose Game — https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/road-to-the-igf-house-house-s-i-untitled-goose-game-i-

principles.principle: Comic structure: set-up, then escalation in visible scale, then payoff, with the size gap between cause and effect as the gag. Keep it 'no one gets hurt'
principles.why_it_works: A tiny cause producing a huge institutional effect is the classic escalation gag. Each rung (whisper, phone, notice, newspaper, cancelled festival) must look bigger than the last so the player feels the snowball. Tonal contrast sharpens it, and keeping harm low keeps it funny rather than mean.
principles.evidence: House House kept a list of slapstick gags (e.g. 'cause a fight between two people') and matched them to each area's setting. The goose is mischievous, 'no one gets hurt'. The sound designer says the harsh honk is funnier because the ambience is pleasant and understated. The GDC 2025 talk 'Comedy Through Patterns' argues comedy comes from structure, level design and music, not only writing. IOI calls Hitman a slapstick comedy among its tones.
sources: Road to the IGF: Untitled Goose Game — https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/road-to-the-igf-house-house-s-i-untitled-goose-game-i-

principles.principle: Timing is performed: stop-start, silence and a beat of hold before the reveal; the score follows real events like a pianist watching
principles.why_it_works: Comic timing (the pause before the punchline, the delayed double take) sets up the expectation that the reveal releases. Model latency of 5–40 s is VIRAL's biggest timing risk. Staged honestly as 'someone is deciding', it becomes anticipation instead of dead air.
principles.evidence: Goose's reactive Debussy score was cut into 400+ fragments. It can jump up or down in intensity or pause into silence, and reviewers said it feels like someone is watching your game. House House found players responded to its stop-start quality more than to reactivity as such. Halo dropped randomness in favour of 'analog reactions' driven by position and timing. Timing is one of Disney's 12 principles.

principles.principle: Minimal cues and apophenia: a few primal, exaggerated body parameters plus gibberish voice, and players supply the rest
principles.why_it_works: People read intent and emotion into moving shapes (Michotte's balls). Low-poly characters need no new art, only a handful of layered procedural parameters per primal emotion (lean, speed, bounce, pauses, head height). Gibberish speech leaves room for the imagination.
principles.evidence: Sylvester: favour simple primal emotions, and the simulation only needs the equivalent of moving balls. Will Wright says offloading part of the simulation to the player's imagination is the goal of Simlish. The Sims 4 shipped mood walk styles and roughly 320 emotion animations so mood can be read from the body rather than the UI. Perlin's Improv uses layered, continuous, non-repetitive procedural motion driven by mood. David Rosen's GDC 2014 procedural animation used about 13 keyframes in total.
