principles.principle: Causal closure: satisfaction and sharing come from tracing the whole chain back to 'my one sentence', and the chain must be real
principles.why_it_works: In Hitman the payoff is watching your set-up trigger, and you know exactly why it worked. A receipt built from the validated event log gives the 'I did that?!' moment and a shareable artifact. Because nothing is faked, it holds up to scrutiny, and players punish visible contrivance.
principles.evidence: Game Maker's Toolkit notes that Hitman characters have very useful conversations the moment 47 is in earshot. It calls this one of the few ways the game feels scripted and gamey, so players notice and devalue convenient coincidences. Halo built a 'real perception, no cheating, can be fooled' knowledge model to keep AI believable. Sylvester's 'story-richness' is the share of interactions that are interesting, so surface the interesting hops and compress the rest.
sources: GMTK, The Making of Hitman 2's Miami Level (transcript) — https://amara.org/subtitles/grmg8UPEXjYO/en/1/download/The%20Making%20of%20Hitman%202s%20Miami%20Level%20%20Game%20Makers%20Toolkit.en.txt

mechanisms.name: Mood posture layer
mechanisms.what: Map each named resident's model `feeling` to 7 primal moods (calm, excited, worried, angry, smug, scared, doubtful) with a keyword table, or add an optional `mood` enum to the JSON schema and fall back to keywords, then neutral. In useFrame, add offsets on top of locomotion and blend them with damped lerp (~0.35 s). Lean rotation.x: excited +0.12, angry +0.18 with shoulders up, worried -0.05 with head pitched down 0.25. Bob frequency/amplitude: excited ×1.6, scared small 2× jitter. Walk speed: angry ×1.4, worried ×0.8 with a 0.3 s micro-stop every 2–3 s, doubtful stops and looks back. Squash scale.y: smug 1.04, scared 0.92. Stance confidence drives gait: below 0.4 gives hesitation stops and head shakes, above 0.8 a straight beeline. Exaggerate about 1.5× what looks natural up close, because the camera is at town scale.
mechanisms.serves: Minimal cues/apophenia; hidden state made visible
mechanisms.risks: Free-text feelings can map to the wrong mood, so keep it to 7 buckets with a neutral default. Pushed too far it looks jittery, so clamp the offsets.

mechanisms.name: Intent telegraph with head-leads-body
mechanisms.what: After a decision is validated and before each action executes: hold still 0.25 s, yaw the head to the target person or place, follow with the body 0.2 s later, then play a 0.4–0.6 s anticipation pose per action type. phone: hand to pocket, phone prop pops 0→1.2→1, raise to ear. tell/ask: lean toward the target, then walk. go look/inspect: hand-visor plus two head sweeps. post notice/publish article: paper prop flourish. public statement/rally: step up, arms raise. cancel festival/close stage/dispatch police: exhale sag (spine -0.15 for 0.5 s), then a decisive nod. Show an intent chip above the head ('→ phoning Tom') with at most one clause of the real inner thought, plus a dashed thread toward the target that turns solid on contact.
mechanisms.serves: Telegraph intent/suspense; hidden state made visible
mechanisms.risks: Adds about 1 s per action; skip the pose when the same actor repeats the same action. Captions must quote only real model fields.

mechanisms.name: Reception double take keyed to real stance change
mechanisms.what: When a resident receives a tell or phone call, stop their routine. If the stance confidence change is at least 0.3, or the topic is new to them: glance at the speaker (0.12 s), look back to the routine (0.35 s), snap the head back (0.08 s, ease-out-back), body jolt with scale.y 1.15→0.9→1, then an emote billboard chosen by resulting stance: '!' for believe, '?' for doubt, red puff for angry, sweat drop for worried. For a small change, just a nod or shrug. Then a thought bubble with the real inner thought, trimmed to about 12 words.
mechanisms.serves: Reaction is the punchline; routine baseline; comic timing
mechanisms.risks: Repetition kills the gag, so gate the full double take on surprise and vary the timing a little based on mood, not randomness.

mechanisms.name: Honest thinking beat that masks model latency
mechanisms.what: While a Gemma call for resident X is pending, X stops and plays a ponder idle: head tilt sine at 0.4 Hz ±0.15 rad, weight shift, an occasional glance toward whoever just told them. Show an animated '…' bubble with no content. A small edge chip reads 'deciding: Mira 12s, Tom 4s'. The director cuts away to already-resolved beats or to the crowd. When the JSON arrives, cut back with a 0.3 s 'lightbulb' beat (head up, small hop) and only then reveal the content.
mechanisms.serves: Timing/anticipation; honesty about what is real
mechanisms.risks: 40 s waits still drag if nothing else is resolved; keep ambient routines and pets visible and let walks fast-forward. Never show placeholder thoughts.

mechanisms.name: Rumour mutation trail
mechanisms.what: Pin the player's exact sentence at the top. Each validated tell/phone/publish/statement appends a card to a horizontal strip: speaker avatar → listener avatar, the claim as the model phrased it, topic tag, confidence bar. Highlight content words not present in the previous hop (token set difference minus stopwords, max 4 highlights). Show a red 'topic changed' tag when the topic differs. Add a counter such as '4 hops · 2 distortions'. Clicking a card focuses the camera on that person.
mechanisms.serves: Dramatic irony via mutation; causal closure
mechanisms.risks: Paraphrase makes diffs noisy, so highlight only nouns and verbs and the topic change. The strip must not overlap captions on small screens.

mechanisms.name: Crowd look-at wave
mechanisms.what: On validated public or institutional events (statement, notice, article, rally, police dispatch, stage closed, festival cancelled), emit a pulse {pos, radius 15–30 m by rung}. Background agents in range start reacting after delay = dist/10 + 0–0.15 s. They stop for 1–2.5 s and yaw head and body toward the source; about 20% pop a '!' sprite and pets bark and hop. For rung-4 events a few walk toward the source, then everyone resumes routine. Attention only: no speech, no belief or claim changes.
mechanisms.serves: Reaction is the punchline; escalation visible in scale
mechanisms.risks: Could imply townsfolk now believe the rumour; keep reactions to looking and pausing. Performance is trivial (yaw lerp).

mechanisms.name: Ending receipt and comic deflation for dead rumours
mechanisms.what: Build the end card from the event log only: the player's sentence → people reached, hops, calls, public acts, and the biggest consequence with an icon. Include the mutation strip and the 'wildest reinterpretation' (the hop with the most change). Buttons: 'Same sentence, different person', 'New sentence', 'Copy result' (text first; image via a canvas created with preserveDrawingBuffer). When the rumour dies, the last listener does a shrug (shoulders up 0.4 s plus head shake), the bubble pops with a 'pfft', and a descending 2-note tone plays. The card is titled 'Nobody bought it' and shows who stopped it, with their real inner-thought reason.
mechanisms.serves: Causal closure/shareability; turns flat endings into a punchline; retry
mechanisms.risks: Image capture can be fiddly; ship text copy first. Keep the card to one screen.

mechanisms.name: Escalation-reactive score (WebAudio)
mechanisms.what: Four synthesized loop layers at about 96 bpm in a pentatonic scale: a triangle-osc pluck with fast decay, a sine bass, noise-burst percussion, and a pad. Intensity is the highest rung reached by real events: 0 ambient, 1 tell, 2 phone/ask/go look, 3 notice/article/statement, 4 police/close stage/cancel festival/rally. A new layer enters on the next bar, preceded by a half-bar dropout (silence before the punchline) and a stinger chord. During a thinking beat, thin to a drone. On ending, a resolve cadence, or the deflate tone when the rumour dies. Include a master volume and mute.
mechanisms.serves: Timing (the Goose piano that seems to watch you); escalation
mechanisms.risks: Can get annoying, so keep gain low and loops sparse. The score must never rise ahead of a real event.

mechanisms.name: Reaction-shot camera grammar
mechanisms.what: Director rules. tell/phone: two-shot framing both people, then shift to the listener 0.2 s before the line ends and hold through the double take. Public events: ease out to a wide shot so the crowd wave reads. Rung-4 event: slow push-in on the prop with a 0.6 s hold. Moves use damped springs, at most one move per 1.2 s. Any user drag or orbit hands control back for 8 s, and the camera never moves while the input box is focused.
mechanisms.serves: Staging; reaction is the punchline; telegraph intent
mechanisms.risks: Motion sickness and fights with player control; keep the moves gentle and easy to cancel.

mechanisms.name: Simlish voice blips synced to captions
mechanisms.what: Give each resident a base pitch (110–330 Hz) and waveform. Captions type on at about 30 chars/s, with a 40–60 ms blip every 3 characters. Pitch contour by mood: questions end rising, angry is lower and louder with jitter, excited is higher, scared gets tremolo. Cap at 12 blips per line.
mechanisms.serves: Apophenia (offloading to imagination); timing
mechanisms.risks: Gets grating when lines overlap; one speaker voiced at a time, low gain.

mechanisms.name: Slapstick prop squash, overshoot and follow-through
mechanisms.what: Every prop spawn (phone, notice, newspaper, stage tape, police sign, festival sign) scales 0→1.15→0.97→1 over 0.35 s. A notice slaps on with a board wobble (spring rotation 0.1 rad, decaying). Tape unrolls with a lagging end, and the newspaper flutters. Hats or hair get a spring child bounce on stops.
mechanisms.serves: Comic structure/satisfaction; follow-through and secondary action
mechanisms.risks: Low; keep overshoot small so it doesn't read as glitchy.

mechanisms.name: Punchline hold on the biggest consequence
mechanisms.what: Once per story, when it first reaches its highest rung (normally rung 4): a 0.5 s pause, then timeScale 0.35 for 0.8 s with a vignette or letterbox, a stamped caption from the real event ('FESTIVAL CANCELLED') with squash, then resume.
mechanisms.serves: Comic timing; escalation payoff
mechanisms.risks: Overuse flattens it; strictly once per story.

mechanisms.name: Threads as tension ropes
mechanisms.what: Upgrade the existing threads to springy beziers: slack while the actor is in their anticipation pose, snap taut with overshoot on contact. A pulse travels from speaker to listener, colour shows the listener's resulting stance (believe/doubt/reject), and the thread fades to dotted once the claim is passed on.
mechanisms.serves: Causal closure; telegraph intent
mechanisms.risks: Visual clutter with many hops; fade older threads.

mechanisms.name: Overheard hooks before typing
mechanisms.what: Clicking a resident before typing shows one authored ambient line drawn from their existing knowledge or relationship data, plus a brief glance toward a person they care about. This gives Hitman-style hooks to aim a sentence at. No model call, no new data.
mechanisms.serves: Retry/anticipation (player sets up the chain)
mechanisms.risks: Spoils secrets if too explicit; hint, don't state.

mechanisms.name: Pet secondary action
mechanisms.what: Pets mirror their owner's current mood: tail-wag speed, hiding behind the owner when the owner is angry or scared, hopping when excited, and a bark on owner double takes.
mechanisms.serves: Reactions/apophenia; secondary action as comic relief
mechanisms.risks: Low.

mechanisms.name: 2× replay from the event log
mechanisms.what: Re-run the director over the recorded validated events with time-compressed walks and no model calls, for re-watching and screen-capture sharing.
mechanisms.serves: Causal closure/shareability
mechanisms.risks: Director state must be replayable deterministically; skip if the director mutates global state.

avoid: Padding playtime: longer walks, forced waits, extra model calls to lengthen stories, unlocks or progression systems

Fake drama: music or crowd reactions that run ahead of real events, 'thinking' text shown before the JSON arrives, background townsfolk voicing claims or new causes, staged coincidences (players notice and discount 'convenient' overheard lines, as GMTK notes of Hitman)
Hidden cognition: model reasoning that never reaches the screen; and its opposite, walls of JSON or inner monologue (one line per beat)
Subtlety at town scale: tiny head turns and 2-degree leans are invisible (Halo lists subtlety as a thing to avoid); exaggerate
Random idle noise posing as personality (Halo dropped randomness and a 'fuzzy' emotion system); drive variation from real mood and stance
Several beats at once (a 'hairball'): one focal beat at a time, the rest as small icons or the queue chip
Repeating one gag: a full double take on every reception, a stinger on every event, slow-mo more than once per story
A camera that takes control while the player types or orbits
Mean-spirited or violent visuals (police dispatch stays comic and civic); keep the goose rule that no one gets hurt
Loud or harsh default audio, or no mute

principles.principle: Encode film grammar as small idioms keyed by event type, kept separate from the code that places the camera.
principles.why_it_works: Viewers read who is talking to whom from standard framings (two-shot, over-the-shoulder, reaction shot) without effort. That frees their attention for the question that matters: 'why did she do THAT?' A short table of idioms gives coherent coverage of emergent events without authoring each scene.
principles.evidence: The Virtual Cinematographer (He, Cohen and Salesin, SIGGRAPH 1996) encodes film idioms as small hierarchical finite state machines: states are shots, transitions are cuts. Shared camera modules (apex, closeapex, external with the near actor at about two-thirds of the screen) do the geometry. For 3 actors it alternates an over-the-shoulder group shot with a reaction shot, then singles, and re-establishes the group now and then. A new development in the scene requires a re-establishing shot. When the actor moves, the camera comes to rest a little before the actor. When something unforeseen happens, control returns to a more general idiom.

principles.principle: Continuity: keep each pair's left-right relation fixed, never jump-cut, cut on the onset of motion, and let sound run continuously across cuts.
principles.why_it_works: Cuts go unnoticed when attention is captured by new motion and the audio carries on. Crossing the line between two people or making a small same-subject cut reads as a glitch and breaks the sense that this is one connected chain of events.
principles.evidence: Smith's Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity explains match-on-action, shot/reverse-shot and the 180-degree rule through attention. His 2017 follow-up with Martin-Portugues Santacreu found that removing post-cut motion made cuts easier to detect, and that edit blindness largely disappeared without audio. Galvane et al. (AAAI 2015) set the jump-cut threshold at a view-angle change of at least 30 degrees or a clear size change, and penalise any flip of left-right order between foreground pairs. Film convention is that two people in shot/reverse-shot face opposite screen directions.

principles.principle: Bound shot length: about 2 s minimum, 8 s maximum, about 4 s typical. Cut faster with closer framing at high intensity, and slower with wider framing when calm.
principles.why_it_works: Under about 2 s the viewer cannot parse the frame, let alone read a caption. Past about 8 s a static frame goes dead. Rhythm itself carries emotion: quick close cuts read as urgency, long wide holds read as consequence and calm.
principles.evidence: Valve's SourceTV/HLTV auto-director (hltvdirector.h) hard-codes MIN_SHOT_LENGTH 2.0, MAX_SHOT_LENGTH 8.0 and DEF_SHOT_LENGTH 4.0 seconds, and uses 2.0 s shots for hurt and death events. Galvane et al. model shot length as log-normal: the original film averaged 6.6 s, and the generated fast and slow edits averaged 2 s and 10 s. Fast cutting favours close and medium shots; slow cutting favours long and full shots. Cinemachine ClearShot has 'Min Duration' (hold unless a higher-priority camera wins) and 'Activate After' settings.

principles.principle: Rank events, look ahead to get into position, and only let a much more important event interrupt. Never use the lookahead to show an outcome before its cause.
principles.why_it_works: When the camera arrives just before the action, the viewer feels that something is about to happen. If the camera shows the result first, the surprise is gone. In VIRAL it would also imply a false cause, because the shot order would no longer match the causal order.
principles.evidence: The HLTV director runs about 30 s behind live play and searches the next 2, 4, 6 and 8 s of logged events, with the comment 'check the next 8 seconds for interrupts/important events'. If the best event is too far ahead, it shows a nearer one. A human cameraman holds a 'record' lock that overrides it. Valve rejected PGL's delayed-observer system for CS:GO because switching to the player about to win a fight gave the result away (Syfy).

principles.principle: Tell a story rather than show everything: favour the person who can change the outcome.
principles.why_it_works: A single throughline ('the baker told the reporter...') is what makes 'how did it end up like THIS?!' land. Showing every small event flattens the chain into noise.
principles.evidence: Heather Garozzo, a CS:GO and PUBG observer (Kotaku), says 'not every kill matters'. She puts the camera on the player with the best chance of a game-changing play, follows a lone survivor in a 2v1, and has a delay observer gather what was missed for an end-of-round replay. Observers anticipate fights from each player's habits.

principles.principle: Shape intensity into peaks and valleys: sustain each peak briefly, let it fade, then relax.
principles.why_it_works: Contrast makes a peak feel big, while constant intensity numbs the viewer. Holding wide after a big consequence lets its meaning land: that held frame is the 'oh no' moment players share.
principles.evidence: Booth's 'The AI Systems of Left 4 Dead' (Valve, 2009) tracks a 'Survivor Intensity' value. Build Up runs until intensity crosses the peak threshold. Sustain Peak holds full threat for 3-5 s after the peak. Peak Fade lets the current fight play out until there is a natural break. Relax keeps threat minimal for 30-45 s. Booth calls the technique 'structured unpredictability'. RimWorld's storyteller is modelled on this Director, and its colour-coded letters (blue good, grey neutral, yellow bad, red threat) each offer a jump-to.

principles.principle: Show simultaneous events in an inset (picture-in-picture) instead of yanking the main camera away.
principles.why_it_works: Seeing 'meanwhile, across town' together with the cause on screen is what makes a spread feel connected. Hard cuts back and forth lose the viewer's sense of place.
principles.evidence: Hitman 2 (2018) uses picture-in-picture for events elsewhere in the level, such as a body being found or a security camera spotting you, without taking you out of play. Director Jacob Mikkelsen describes it as a way to keep players informed while balancing how much data they get against overload. The feature dates back to Hitman: Blood Money.

principles.principle: Make waits on the model occupied, explained and staged as suspense. Fill dead time with real replays and real state, never with invented action.
principles.why_it_works: Unoccupied, unexplained and uncertain waits feel longer. A short hold on someone thinking reads as a drumroll; a long frozen one reads as a crash. Sports broadcasts fill stoppages with replays and the scoreboard, which keeps viewers watching without inventing anything.
principles.evidence: Maister's 'The Psychology of Waiting Lines' (1985): occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time, uncertain waits feel longer than known, finite waits, and unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones. Larson (MIT) reports that people overestimate how long they waited by about 36%. In esports, a delay observer packages missed moments for the end-of-round replay. Left 4 Dead's Relax phase is a deliberate low-intensity valley rather than dead air.

principles.principle: Put frame coherence ahead of perfect framing, and hand control to the player instantly, resuming only after they stop.
principles.why_it_works: A camera that solves for the best framing every frame jitters, and a camera that fights the player's input disorients them. Watch-games are mostly lean-back, but the player needs to be able to lean in (look around) and have the director pick up again without a jolt.
principles.evidence: Halper, Helbing and Strothotte (Eurographics 2001) found that 'optimal constraint satisfaction tends to lead to the camera jumping around too much', so they trade constraint satisfaction against frame coherence. HLTV's human-cameraman 'record' lock overrides the auto-director. Cinemachine's recentering waits a set time after the last input and then eases back over a set time. Nesky's GDC talk '50 Camera Mistakes' catalogues automatic-camera failures and fixes.

principles.principle: Establish before going close, re-establish when the action moves somewhere new, and end on the whole picture.
principles.why_it_works: The rumour's spread is a spatial story. Establishing shots give the player a mental map, so a cut 'to the police station' means something, and a final wide shot of every thread becomes the shareable answer to 'how did it end up like this'.
principles.evidence: The Virtual Cinematographer establishes a scene before close shots and re-establishes on any new development. Esports productions open with map flyovers before the match (Kotaku). The HLTV director uses fixed cameras for round start and end, and picks one on 25% of random shots when static shots are allowed.

mechanisms.name: Shot record, priority table and hold rules (core director)
mechanisms.what:
In src/town/director.ts, replace `show.focus: string` with `show.shot = {kind, a, b?, size, prio, eventId, start, minUntil}` behind one call, `requestShot(spec)`. CameraRig in TownScene.tsx (lines 43-104) reads the shot instead of an npc name. Keep `show.focus` as a derived alias so PlaybackLayer's ring highlight still works.

Priorities:
- P5: cancel festival, dispatch police, close stage, rally, publish article.
- P4: public statement, post notice, close shop.
- P3: tell, phone, ask, and the listener's reaction.
- P2: go look, inspect.
- P1: thinking and inner-thought captions.
- P0: ambient townsfolk and pets, used only while waiting on the model.
- +1 when the event flips a stance, touches a resident's secret, or comes from a resident whose role can trigger a P5 action (mayor, police, journalist).

Holds:
- minHold = max(2.0 s, the existing readTime(caption)), capped at 6 s.
- maxHold = 8 s. After that, reframe on the same side of the pair's line: rotate the azimuth 35 degrees or change size by one step.
- A new request interrupts only if newPrio is at least curPrio + 2 and the current shot is at least 1.0 s old. P5 interrupts any non-P5 shot after 0.6 s.
- Otherwise the request waits in a queue of at most 3; drop entries older than 6 s whose priority is below 3.
- Every shot must carry the id of a real event, or be a labelled filler (wait, map, replay).
mechanisms.serves: Idioms; shot-length bounds; priority and interruption; storytelling over completeness.
mechanisms.risks: Long captions plus queued shots could fall behind playback; skip the queue and cut straight to the newest event when playback is more than one event ahead. The existing focusLater phone cut must route through requestShot.

mechanisms.name: Framing ladder and shot per event type
mechanisms.what:
Size ladder for the current fov of 32 degrees (visible height is about 0.57 x distance):
- CLOSE: 9 m, pitch 22 degrees.
- MEDIUM: 15 m, pitch 30 degrees.
- WIDE: 28 m, pitch 38 degrees (the current FOLLOW_DISTANCE).
- ESTABLISH: the existing VIEWS entry for the district.
- OVERVIEW: VIEWS.overview.
Keep the player's last azimuth unless the line rule (next mechanism) says otherwise.

Two-shot: target = lerp(speaker, listener, 0.45); d = clamp(1.3 x separation + 8, 9, 30). If the separation is over 22 m, do not use a two-shot; cross-cut or use the inset instead.
Over-the-shoulder: camera at listener + 4 m along (listener - speaker), +3 m up, 1.2 m to the side, looking at the speaker.

Shots by event:
- Story start: ESTABLISH 2.0 s on the clicked resident's district, then CUT to CLOSE on that resident hearing the sentence.
- tell/ask: MEDIUM two-shot for the line, then CUT to an over-the-shoulder shot of the listener when their inner thought appears.
- phone: CLOSE on the caller, then CUT to CLOSE on the receiver at about 55% of the line (existing behaviour), keeping mirrored screen sides.
- go look/inspect: WIDE follow with lead room (target = position + velocity x 1.0 s). If the walk lasts more than 6 s, CUT ahead to the real destination so the actor walks into frame.
- notice/close shop/statement: MEDIUM on the actor, then WIDE on the prop plus nearby crowd for 3 s.
- P5: CLOSE on the decider for at least 1.5 s while the decision caption shows, then a hard cut plus sound sting to ESTABLISH on the affected site, held 3-5 s.
- thinking: CLOSE with a slow push-in of 8% over 5 s.
- end: OVERVIEW with every thread, 4 s.
mechanisms.serves: Idioms (two-shot, over-the-shoulder, reaction shot); camera resting ahead of the moving actor; sustain-peak hold; establish then re-establish.
mechanisms.risks: Buildings can block close shots; if a raycast from camera to head hits a building, step up one size. Low-poly faces carry little expression, so close shots depend on the bubble and caption.

mechanisms.name: Per-pair line of interest and jump-cut guard
mechanisms.what:
When a pair (A,B) is first framed in a story, store side = sign(cross(B - A, camera - A).y) in a Map keyed by the pair. Every later two-shot, over-the-shoulder or phone cross-cut for that pair places the camera on that side, so A stays screen-left of B for the whole story. On the phone cross-cut, the caller faces screen-right and the receiver screen-left.

Jump-cut guard: if the new shot has the same subject, the azimuth changes by less than 30 degrees and the size changes by less than one step, blend instead of cutting, or keep the current shot.
mechanisms.serves: Continuity (180-degree rule, no jump cuts).
mechanisms.risks: Moving actors can swing the line mid-shot. Recompute the side only between shots, never during one.

mechanisms.name: Choosing cut, blend or travel
mechanisms.what:
- CUT: for a new subject more than 20 m away, any reaction shot, or any interrupt. Time it to the frame where the new subject's gesture starts (raise phone, turn head), so the cut lands on motion.
- BLEND: smoothstep over 0.8 s for the same subject or the same area (under 20 m), and for size changes.
- TRAVEL: an arc of 1.4 s that rises 15 m at mid-flight, used only the first time a district enters the story, so the geography is shown once. Later returns CUT.
Keep the WebAudio ambience bed continuous across every cut. Play a soft whoosh only on travel.
Replace the current 'k = 1 - exp(-dt * 2.2)' chase with these explicit transitions, keeping a light 0.15 s damping on the target to absorb walking jitter.
mechanisms.serves: Cutting on motion and audio continuity; frame coherence; establishing geography.
mechanisms.risks: Too many travel arcs feel slow, so cap them at 2 per story. Over a 40 s story, cuts at a 2 s minimum could reach 20; that is acceptable only if captions stay readable.

mechanisms.name: Wait choreography for model calls
mechanisms.what:
Driven by show.stalled and show.thinking (director.ts lines 453-473), with a timeline measured from the start of the stall:
- 0-4 s: CLOSE on the thinker with a slow push-in. Keep the existing thinking bubble and add an honest elapsed counter to the caption, for example '阿美正在想…… 12 秒' (Amei is thinking... 12 s).
- 4-12 s: blend to MEDIUM with a 6 degree/s orbit around the thinker, plus a quiet WebAudio tick or heartbeat.
- 12-20 s: CUT to a map shot (ESTABLISH or OVERVIEW) with the real threads and infected rings visible, captioned '目前 3 人知道' (3 people know so far), at most 6 s.
- 20 s and later: a labelled REPLAY ('重播' tag, slightly desaturated) of the highest-priority event so far, re-shot from an angle 35 degrees off but on the same side, 6 s. Then return to the thinker and loop map and replay.
- When the result arrives: respect the current shot's 1 s minimum, then CUT to the thinker on their reaction animation (head snap) with a sting, then show the inner-thought caption.
- Several thinkers: the main shot goes to the one with the highest role bonus, and the next one goes to the inset if it exists.
mechanisms.serves: Occupied, explained waits; peak and valley pacing; replay as honest filler; suspense payoff.
mechanisms.risks: Replays must be clearly marked or players will think the event happened twice. Ambient townsfolk shots must not be intercut in a way that implies they heard the rumour. Model latency varies between 5 and 40 s, so every phase must be interruptible.

mechanisms.name: Player takeover and edge indicators
mechanisms.what:
On OrbitControls 'start', the director yields immediately, like HLTV's cameraman lock. Show a chip: '導演暫停 · 6 秒後恢復 · [F] 跟拍' (Director paused · resumes in 6 s · [F] to follow). After 6 s with no input, resume with a 1 s blend into the current shot, as Cinemachine's Wait/Time recentering does.

While the player has control, events at P4 or above that happen off-screen show an edge arrow with the resident's name and the event icon, coloured by priority (RimWorld-style letter). Clicking the arrow or an event-log line CUTs to that event's shot. The existing ui.follow toggle stays as the master switch.
mechanisms.serves: Yielding to the player; frame coherence; jump-to without disorientation.
mechanisms.risks: Resuming during a drag must not happen; reset the 6 s timer on every input event, including wheel.

mechanisms.name: Picture-in-picture inset for simultaneous events
mechanisms.serves: Simultaneous events without yanking; cause and effect across space.
mechanisms.risks: A second render costs GPU time with about 90 agents and shadows, so disable shadows in the inset and render it at half resolution. Skip it on mobile widths.

mechanisms.name: Intensity-driven cutting tempo
mechanisms.what:
intensity += prio squared on each event and decays by 15% per second.
- intensity above 20: minHold 1.6 s, prefer CLOSE or MEDIUM.
- intensity below 5: holds of 4-6 s, prefer WIDE, ambience slightly louder.
- After a P5 event: a mandatory 3-5 s ESTABLISH hold (sustain peak), then 'relax', where the next P3 or lower event is framed one size wider.
mechanisms.serves: Peak and valley pacing (Left 4 Dead Director); rhythm matched to shot size (Galvane et al.).
mechanisms.risks: Tuning time; keep it to one function with two thresholds.

mechanisms.name: End frame and highlight replay
mechanisms.what:
When the story ends:
- OVERVIEW for 4 s with every thread drawn and infected rings lit.
- A title overlay built from real counts, for example '1 句話 → 6 人 → 節慶取消' (1 sentence → 6 people → festival cancelled).
- A [重播精華] (highlight replay) button that replays the top 3 events at P4 or above, 3 s each, using their stored shot specs and labelled REPLAY.
- A [截圖] (screenshot) button that renders one frame and calls gl.domElement.toBlob.
mechanisms.serves: Satisfaction, sharing, 'how did it end up like THIS'; re-establishing at the end.
mechanisms.risks: toBlob without preserveDrawingBuffer returns a blank image unless it is called right after a render in the same frame. A story that dies after one hop needs an honest small end frame ('傳到 1 人就停了', it stopped after reaching 1 person) rather than a padded one.

mechanisms.name: Sound leading the cut (J-cut)
mechanisms.what: Schedule the next event's sound (phone ring, door, crowd murmur, notice-board hammer) on the WebAudio clock 0.4 s before the planned visual CUT. The ear arrives first and the cut feels motivated.
mechanisms.serves: Audio continuity hides cuts; anticipation.
mechanisms.risks: It needs the cut time to be known ahead, which planned cuts already provide. Do not apply it to interrupts.

mechanisms.name: Anticipatory pre-roll without spoilers
mechanisms.what:
Events before show.frontier are final. In the last 0.8 s of the current shot, start blending toward a framing that includes the next event's actor (not its outcome location), so the actor is already in frame when the cut lands.
Never pre-roll to a P4/P5 consequence site (stage, police, newspaper) before the decision caption has played.
mechanisms.serves: Lookahead without spoilers; shot order matches causal order.
mechanisms.risks: Pre-rolling onto the next listener can hint at who gets told next, which is mild and acceptable. Pre-rolling onto outcomes is not allowed.

avoid: Shots shorter than the caption's reading time, or cutting to every background townsperson or pet event; not every event earns a shot.
Pulling the camera away while the player is dragging or zooming, or an auto-zoom that fights their wheel input.
Crossing a pair's line between shots (A suddenly screen-right of B), or same-subject cuts with less than 30 degrees and less than one size step of change (jump cuts).
A smooth cross-town glide for every focus change. Show the geography once with a travel arc, then cut; repeated glides are dead time and cause motion sickness.

Using the streamed lookahead to show a consequence (police car, cancelled stage) before the decision that causes it. It spoils the surprise, as Valve found with PGL's delayed observer, and it implies a false cause.
Filler during model waits that looks like story: townsfolk reacting to a rumour they never received, fake 'typing' text, fake progress percentages, unlabelled replays.
Padding playback with slow motion or artificial delays to stretch a short story; a rumour that dies fast gets an honest, short end frame.
Shake, sting or dramatic zoom on minor events. Spend them only on P5 moments or they lose their meaning.
More than one picture-in-picture inset, split screens, or overlays covering the residents being framed.
Building a general camera constraint solver or a Cinemachine clone. A priority table, five sizes and three transition types are enough for a 40 h deadline.
Free camera with no director as the default (players miss the chain), or a director with no instant way for the player to take control.

principles.principle: Curate, don't dump: a simulation log only becomes a story once someone picks the tellable spine and drops the rest.
principles.why_it_works: Raw traces read like a debug log, the 'nonstory' problem. A story needs an interesting endpoint, then a causal chain traced back to the point that needs no explanation (Labov's tellability). Players remember the spine, not the 40 events.
principles.evidence: Ryan argues emergent narrative keeps its computational appeal only through 'a procedure of curation', and that bare simulation traces do not count as narrative. He proposes sifting patterns plus backward chaining from the most interesting final event. Kreminski's Felt and Winnow make this an engineering primitive: queries over the event log that find story-shaped sequences.

principles.principle: Make the social physics legible: every accept or reject shows its reason in the character's own terms.
principles.why_it_works: Anticipation and surprise both need a model of the rules. If players can see why someone refused, they start predicting ('she'll never believe him, they're rivals'). That turns watching into betting, and a violated prediction then lands as surprise instead of noise.
principles.evidence: The Prom Week designers explain outcomes as character reasons, e.g. Simon does not believe Cassandra's rumour about Naomi 'because he is better friends with Naomi'. Reviewers called the system 'social physics' with legible, multi-factor causes. This is the exact rumour-rejection case VIRAL has.

principles.principle: Show the gap between what is said and what is thought (dramatic irony).
principles.why_it_works: When the player can see the inner thought but the listener only hears the words, every line carries double meaning. Lying, hedging, gossip-with-glee and fake politeness become funny or tense with no extra content, and the player feels like an insider.
principles.evidence: Dead Meat builds its core tool, the 'Mind Reader 3000', around this: ask a question, then see what is really going on in the suspect's head. Generative Agents lets the user act as an agent's 'inner voice' and separates the action shown above the head from the full description. Façade's drama lives in subtext between Trip and Grace.

principles.principle: Rumours should visibly mutate hop by hop, and every version should keep its provenance.
principles.why_it_works: The 'how did it end up like THIS' feeling is the telephone game. It needs a visible before and after, plus the exact hop where the meaning changed and who changed it. Embellishment by a named person is both a joke and a cause.
principles.evidence: Talk of the Town is built around what characters know and how knowledge moves between them, including misremembering and lying. Generative Agents reports real embellishment: Isabella confirmed Sam's candidacy but added 'he's going to make an announcement tomorrow', which was never discussed. The authors checked every 'yes' against the dialogue in the memory stream, so the provenance was auditable.

principles.principle: Refusals, doubts and no-shows are content, not failure.
principles.why_it_works: A spread graph that shows who refused, and why, has more texture than one that only shows success. Refusals give each resident a personality and explain why a story stopped. That is what makes a 'nothing happened' run tellable.
principles.evidence: In Smallville, 12 agents were invited to the party and 5 came. Three of the seven absentees cited conflicts (Rajiv was too busy with his show). The paper reports that breakdown as a finding, and it is the most human part of the diffusion result. Ryan's backward chaining stops at 'an event that needs no explanation', so a stopper is a valid story endpoint.

principles.principle: Show diffusion as a path graph, not a counter.
principles.why_it_works: '13 of 25 agents knew' is forgettable. A drawn path from the seed through named people, with branches and dead ends, is something players can point at, retell and screenshot.
principles.evidence: Generative Agents shows its result as Figure 9, the diffusion path of the party invitation, and backs it with numbers (party 1 to 13 agents, candidacy 1 to 8). Project Sid tracked meme and religion spread by detecting keywords in agent conversations, separating direct from indirect converts. The path, not the total, is the explanation.

principles.principle: Indirect influence: the player's words, not commands, become reality, and the payoff is recognising your own words out in the world.
principles.why_it_works: One sentence is a tiny lever. Satisfaction comes from authorship plus loss of control: you see your exact words reappear in the world, twisted, on a notice board or in a headline. It is the same pleasure as 1001 Nights turning spoken words into weapons, or Suck Up! residents reacting to your persuasion.
principles.evidence: 1001 Nights never lets players command the King. They steer him toward keywords, which then materialise as equipment. The authors frame this as 'language as reality' and report data from 2,055 players. Suck Up!'s whole loop is talking AI residents into opening the door, and it spread through clips (it has a meme-encyclopedia entry).

principles.principle: Use minimal representation and trust apophenia: crisp causal cues on simple bodies beat explanation text.
principles.why_it_works: Players project rich emotion onto simple moving shapes once the cause and effect is clear. Over-explaining kills the co-authoring that makes players feel the story is theirs. Short captions plus body language leave room to retell.
principles.evidence: Tynan Sylvester calls apophenia the key to making a simulation work, and advises the minimum representation that supports the stories you want. His GDC 2017 talk describes RimWorld as a story generator where omitted detail is filled in by players.

principles.principle: Pace in beats: every input gets an immediate visible reaction, and story time is compressed between beats.
principles.why_it_works: Dead air kills anticipation. A beat is an action-reaction pair; if the reaction is visible at once, even as 'she frowns, thinking', the wait becomes suspense instead of loading. With 5-40 s model calls, VIRAL must perform the waiting.
principles.evidence: Façade structures drama as beats, the smallest unit of value change, and its beat manager picks the next beat to fit the dramatic arc. Thousands of joint dialog behaviours give instant reactions. Note that Ryan rejects hidden drama managers on aesthetic grounds: managed events 'do not feel like they actually happen'. So use beats for presentation only, never to steer outcomes.

principles.principle: Incremental, in-progress recognition creates anticipation ('a story is forming').
principles.why_it_works: Suspense needs the viewer to see a story partly assembled: a loaded gun on the table. Pointing out real, partially matched patterns, such as the person who can cancel the festival now believing the claim, creates tension without faking.
principles.evidence: Winnow (AIIDE 2021) was built because earlier sifters only recognised storyful sequences once they had fully played out. It tracks partial matches while they unfold, so in-progress stories can be surfaced. Awash-style work feeds candidate stories to presentation during play.

principles.principle: Retellings are the success metric, so design the run's end as a ready-made retelling.
principles.why_it_works: Players share stories, not simulations. If the game hands over a compact, correct retelling (headline, chain, quote), sharing costs nothing. Dwarf Fortress players spread its legends by retelling them from traces.
principles.evidence: Eladhari's ICIDS 2018 best paper argues that players' re-tellings are the 'fourth layer' of narrative, and that how often they happen indicates a well-designed system. The 'That Darned Sandstorm' study shows players building stories from procedural traces, archaeology-style.

mechanisms.name: Three-layer hop caption (HEARD / THOUGHT / VERDICT)
mechanisms.what: For each tell or phone event, run three short beats over the receiver. (1) A speech bubble quoting the sender's exact claim text from the event. (2) A dimmer italic thought cloud with the receiver's own inner_thought, cut to 12 words or fewer. (3) A stamp that drops in with a 120 ms scale-bounce: BELIEVES / DOUBTS / WILL CHECK / REFUSES / SHRUGS. The stamp comes from the stance confidence (>=0.7 believes, 0.4-0.7 doubts, <0.4 refuses) plus whether an inspect, ask or go-look action was chosen (WILL CHECK). Hover shows the raw confidence.
mechanisms.serves: Legible social physics; said-vs-thought dramatic irony; refusals as content
mechanisms.risks: Text overload if several hops overlap; queue them and show one focal hop at a time. If inner_thought is empty or generic, skip the cloud rather than pad it.

mechanisms.name: Mutation diff and version tag
mechanisms.what: When a resident retells, take a word-level LCS diff of their claim against the parent claim they received (engine message parent id). Highlight up to 3 added or changed content words in amber, and briefly flash removed words with a strikethrough. Tag the bubble 'v3, changed by Ben'. If word similarity is under 0.3, label it 'retold in own words' instead of diffing. Keep a small top-of-screen ticker with the current most-spread version.
mechanisms.serves: Hop-by-hop mutation with provenance; the 'how did it end up like this' moment
mechanisms.risks: Paraphrase noise produces meaningless highlights. Mitigate with a stop-word filter, a cap of 3 highlights, and the similarity fallback. It must use only real claim strings.

mechanisms.name: Performed thinking beat during model latency
mechanisms.what: While a resident's LLM call is pending: they stop, turn to face the source (yaw lerp), and tilt their head with a slow sine bob. A thought cloud shows only animated dots, never content. The camera eases into a two-shot and a soft WebAudio drone fades in. After 12 s, the director cuts to other real queued events or ambient townsfolk, returning with a 'still thinking' marker. When the result arrives, a short pop sound plays and the HEARD/THOUGHT/VERDICT beat runs.
mechanisms.serves: Beat pacing (Façade); turn latency into suspense
mechanisms.risks: Must never hint at the outcome before it exists: dots only, neutral face. Long waits can still drag; cap total idle by cutting away.

mechanisms.name: Spine sifter (backward chaining over the real log)
mechanisms.what: After the run, rank events by consequence: cancel festival > dispatch police > close stage > publish article > public statement > rally > close shop > post notice > tell/phone > inspect. Take the top event and walk parent links back to the player's sentence; that chain is the spine. Spine hops get the camera priority flag (rendered thicker in the thread view) and drive the headline and the end-card tree highlight. About 40 lines of code: a parent pointer on every engine event.
mechanisms.serves: Curation over simulation (Ryan, Felt/Winnow)
mechanisms.risks: Needs reliable causal parent ids on every event. Where the engine lacks one, show the event but leave it off the spine. Never guess causes.

mechanisms.name: Stance-colored threads as a live spread map
mechanisms.what: Reuse the existing threads. Colour each by the receiver's verdict: green solid (believes), amber dashed (doubts or will check), grey thin (refuses, ignored), red pulse (acted). Threads persist faintly for the whole run, so a wide shot shows the real diffusion graph with branches and dead ends.
mechanisms.serves: Diffusion as a path graph; refusals visible
mechanisms.risks: Clutter with 16+ threads; fade non-spine threads to 30% opacity after 10 s.

mechanisms.name: Town Gazette end card (shareable artifact)
mechanisms.what: A 2D overlay, exportable as PNG via canvas toDataURL plus a copy button. It contains: (1) a template headline built from log fields, e.g. '{Actor} {action-verb} after {N} neighbours pass on {player's subject}', or a firewall headline for dead runs. (2) 'You said: "..."' next to 'The town ended up saying: "..."', the final spine claim, with surviving original words in the player's colour. (3) A mutation tree: BFS layers, nodes are resident portraits or initials with a verdict badge, edges labelled v1..vN. (4) Up to 3 real consequences with icons. (5) Stats: heard N, believed M, doubted K, acted A. The model may only be quoted verbatim with attribution; no free LLM summary.
mechanisms.serves: Retellings as the success metric; indirect-influence payoff; shareability
mechanisms.risks: Time. Keep the tree layout naive (layers by hop depth, max 16 nodes). An LLM-written recap would invent causes, so use templates only.

mechanisms.name: Firewall ending for runs that die early
mechanisms.what: If the rumour stops (no pending tells), name the stopper(s): the last receivers whose verdict was DOUBTS/REFUSES/WILL CHECK. Show their inner thought as an epitaph quote and use the headline template 'Rumour about {subject} dies at {Name}'s {workplace}'. Add a 'closest call' line built only from facts: the highest-impact resident who heard it, what their role lets them do, and what they actually did ('The Mayor heard it. She can cancel the festival. She decided to check first.'). Give earned titles from counts: The Megaphone (most tells), The Mutator (biggest diff), The Firewall (stopped it).
mechanisms.serves: Satisfying 'nothing happened' endings; refusals as content
mechanisms.risks: The 'could have' line must state only a role capability that exists in the engine's action set, never a prediction of what would have happened.

mechanisms.name: Loaded-gun markers (in-progress story signals)
mechanisms.what: When a resident who has a high-impact action available (police, mayor, journalist, stage manager) comes to believe the claim at confidence 0.7 or higher, float a small role icon over them (siren / gavel / newspaper) with a slow pulse and a soft WebAudio tick. It resolves visibly: the icon fires into the action, or fades with a 'chose not to' stamp when their decision has no high-impact action.
mechanisms.serves: Incremental sifting creates anticipation (Winnow)
mechanisms.risks: Can read as a promise. It shows capability plus belief, both real state, and always resolves on screen.

mechanisms.name: Word-survival highlight on world props
mechanisms.what: Tokenise the player's original sentence (minus stop words). When those tokens appear on real props (posted notice text, article headline, public statement caption), underline them in the player's colour with a tiny sparkle. On the end card, list 'your words that survived' and 'words the town added'.
mechanisms.serves: Indirect influence: your words become world (1001 Nights)
mechanisms.risks: Low. Purely presentational over real strings. Handle Chinese/English tokenisation simply (split on whitespace and punctuation, plus character n-grams for CJK).

mechanisms.name: Feeling-driven procedural body language
mechanisms.what: Map the feeling field to tiny r3f transforms. Shocked: y-squash and a 0.15 s hop. Doubtful: head-shake yaw sine, 2 cycles. Gleeful or gossipy: lean in 10 degrees and a faster walk. Angry: stomp (bob amplitude x2) and fists via arm rotation. Afraid: back-step 0.3 m. Calm or neutral: idle. Walk speed scales with urgency (tell on foot after a phone call = 1.4x).
mechanisms.serves: Minimal representation and apophenia (RimWorld)
mechanisms.risks: Unknown feeling strings; map with a keyword table and default to neutral. Do not exaggerate beyond the model's stated feeling.

mechanisms.name: WebAudio verdict and escalation motifs
mechanisms.what: Oscillator-only blips under 150 ms. Believe: rising major third. Doubt: falling minor second. Refuse: low muted thud (filtered noise). Mutation: a detuned chirp when the diff finds changes. Act: a low drum hit plus a stamp click. Base pitch rises one semitone per hop depth, so a long chain audibly escalates. Master gain is 0.15, with a mute toggle.
mechanisms.serves: Legible feedback; anticipation through escalation
mechanisms.risks: Annoyance on long runs: throttle to one sound per 300 ms and duck during captions.

mechanisms.name: Director camera rules
mechanisms.what: A few deterministic rules. Hop start: two-shot of sender and receiver. Verdict: 1.2 s hold on the receiver's face. Phone: split framing, receiver first. Public event (notice, article, statement, rally): pull out to a 3/4 bird's-eye so passing background townsfolk are in frame. World-changing action: short push-in plus 2 frames of hit-stop. Non-spine hops play at 1.5x.
mechanisms.serves: Beat pacing; curation (spine gets screen time)
mechanisms.risks: Camera thrash with parallel events; enforce a minimum 1.5 s per shot and a queue.

mechanisms.name: Retry hooks on end card
mechanisms.what: Two buttons: 'Same sentence, different resident' (keeps the text, opens resident picker) and 'Same resident, new sentence'. Show untouched named residents as faded portraits labelled 'never heard it' (real state). One-click replay of the spine only, at 2x.
mechanisms.serves: Desire to retry; curiosity about unexplored branches
mechanisms.risks: Low.

mechanisms.name: Crowd notice reactions (rule-driven townsfolk)
mechanisms.what: When a real public event fires (notice posted, article published, statement, stage closed), background townsfolk within a radius stop, turn toward the source, show a '!' or '?' emoji for 1.5 s, and a few walk over to the notice board. This is pure presentation triggered only by that event; no belief state is implied or counted.
mechanisms.serves: Scale and humour of the mundane town reacting (Two Point / Plague Inc. feel)
mechanisms.risks: Must not show a 'percent of town believes' figure: background folk have no modelled beliefs. Label it as 'saw the notice' only.

mechanisms.name: At-a-glance emoji status above heads
mechanisms.what: In wide shots, replace text with a 1-2 emoji badge per named resident derived from the latest real event type (phone, walking to inspect, store closed, newspaper). This mirrors Smallville's emoji action bubbles; click to expand the full caption.
mechanisms.serves: Minimal representation; readability at distance
mechanisms.risks: Emoji rendering differences across OSes; use a small SVG icon set instead if needed.

mechanisms.name: Secret-in-play reveal
mechanisms.what: If a claim's topic matches a resident's secret topic in engine data, flash a one-time 'X's secret is now in play' card with a lock-breaking sound, and mark that node on the tree. It fires only on an exact engine-side topic match.
mechanisms.serves: Surprise and dramatic irony; shareable twist
mechanisms.risks: False positives from loose topic matching; require an exact topic id match, or skip it.

avoid: An LLM-written recap or headline that summarises the run freely: it will invent motives and causes. Use templates over log fields and quote model text verbatim with attribution.
Padding playback with idle walks, fake extra hops, or invented crowd belief counts to make short runs feel longer. Compress waits and make the short ending tellable instead (firewall, closest call).
Predictive language ('this will cause...', 'the festival is doomed') before the event exists. Show capability plus belief only, and always resolve markers on screen.
Hidden drama-manager nudging (re-prompting, biasing models toward spicier outcomes) to manufacture drama. Ryan: managed events 'do not feel like they actually happen', and it breaks the no-fake rule.
Walls of text: raw JSON, multiple confidence numbers, full inner monologues. Keep each bubble to 12 words or fewer, one focal hop at a time, numbers on hover only.
Showing content in the thinking beat before the model returns (no pre-written reaction lines). Dots and neutral body language only.
Over-highlighting paraphrase noise in diffs. Cap highlights and fall back to 'retold in own words'.
Framing an early-dying rumour as failure ('Game Over', 'Nothing happened'). Present it as a result with a named stopper and quote.
New long-term systems that extend playtime: persistent reputation, unlocks, multi-day campaigns, relationship progression, achievements unrelated to the run log.
Loud or long stingers and dramatic music that imply stakes the log does not contain. Keep sound short, quiet, and tied to real events.
Camera cuts faster than the player can read. Keep at least 1.5 s per shot and hold on verdicts.
Showing belief percentages for the ~90 background townsfolk, who have no modelled beliefs. They can only react visibly to real public events.
